claims.text: A thin chromium-based coating on zirconium-alloy nuclear-fuel cladding will improve resistance to high-temperature oxidation relative to uncoated cladding.
The chromium-based coating will form a protective chromium oxide layer during high-temperature oxidation.
The chromium oxide layer will impede oxygen diffusion into the zirconium-alloy substrate.
Physical vapor deposition is a suitable method for applying the proposed thin chromium-based coating.
The coating will form a dense chromium oxide scale identified as Cr2O3.
The resulting Cr2O3 scale will adhere to the cladding surface.
At elevated temperature, chromium in the coating reacts with oxygen to form a stable chromia scale.
By limiting oxygen ingress, the chromia scale will reduce the oxidation rate of the zirconium-alloy substrate.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, chromium-coated cladding will have a significantly lower oxidation-related weight gain than uncoated cladding.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, chromium-coated cladding will develop a shallower oxide scale than uncoated cladding.
The expected improvement applies approximately over 1000–1200°C for limited exposure durations.
Performance above approximately 1200°C or over extended exposure durations has not been established.
The oxidation-rate reduction could range from a noticeable reduction to an order-of-magnitude decrease.
Long-term coating durability under reactor conditions is uncertain.
Coated and uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding samples will be compared after steam oxidation at around 1200°C.
A lack of statistically significant reduction in weight gain or oxide-scale thickness relative to the uncoated control will falsify the hypothesis.
Poor coating integrity or adhesion after exposure will falsify the hypothesis.
